summary:
CropWise: NASA-Powered Crop Rotation Decision Support

CropWise is a multilingual, mobile-first web app that helps farmers explore crop rotation strategies that protect soil health, conserve water and adapt to changing weather. It detects the field’s live location and pulls NASA data for that exact spot: NASA POWER climate history, NASA GIBS map layers (MODIS NDVI, SMAP, GPM IMERG) and a NASA Data Hub that honestly labels each dataset as live, map layer or planned. It combines these with Open-Meteo forecasts and SoilGrids soil data.

Features include a soil health score, water-balance meter, frost and heat alerts, a rule-based weekly irrigation, spraying and fertilizing timetable, and a three-way rotation comparison with scenario sliders, evidence, risks and data gaps. Farmers can upload a leaf photo for AI disease diagnosis with a confidence estimate, chat with an AI assistant, use voice in English, Hindi and Marathi, log field activity, and connect hardware sensors to compare ground readings with satellite data.

Most influential addition: completing the NASA AppEEARS pipeline, so real MODIS, SMAP and ECOSTRESS time series per field drive the bare-field detection and rotation scores. That would turn the decision support from heuristic into truly satellite-evidence-based.
details:
CropWise: Project Details

What does it do and how does it work?

CropWise is a multilingual decision-support web app that helps farmers explore crop rotation strategies for healthier soil and better water use. The farmer taps Detect my field location (or searches a place name), and the app pulls data for that exact spot: NASA POWER climate history (temperature, rainfall, evapotranspiration, soil wetness), NASA GIBS satellite map layers (MODIS NDVI, SMAP, GPM IMERG), SoilGrids soil properties and a 7-day Open-Meteo forecast.

From this, it produces:

  • a soil health score, water-balance meter and frost, heat and heavy-rain alerts
  • a weekly timetable for irrigation, spraying and fertilizing, built from simple, explainable rules
  • a comparison of three rotations (existing, legume-based, drought-tolerant plus cover crop) with scenario sliders for rainfall and temperature. Each rotation shows why it was suggested, the evidence used, benefits, risks and data gaps
  • AI leaf-photo diagnosis with a confidence estimate, cause and suggested treatment, plus an AI chatbot
  • a NASA Data Hub that labels every dataset honestly as live, map layer or planned

Benefits

Farmers get clear, location-specific guidance in their own language, with voice support for low-literacy users. They can plan field work around weather and compare rotation options before committing a season. Ground sensor readings can be compared with satellite data.

Intended impact

To make NASA Earth observation data usable by smallholder farmers, helping them conserve water, reduce erosion and improve soil health while staying resilient to changing weather. It supports and never replaces farmer judgment and local agronomic expertise, and the app says so on every screen.

Tools and technologies

  • Frontend: React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet maps, Recharts, i18next (English, Hindi, Marathi), Web Speech API
  • Backend and database: Node.js, Express, Supabase (PostgreSQL with Row Level Security)
  • Data sources: NASA POWER, NASA GIBS (MODIS, SMAP, GPM IMERG), NASA AppEEARS, SoilGrids, Open-Meteo
  • AI: Google Gemini API for leaf diagnosis, chat and translation
  • Design and development: Google Stitch (UI design), Google Antigravity, GitHub Copilot, VS Code, GitHub
  • Hardware: environmental sensors sending readings to a secured API endpoint, compared against NASA data

How is it creative?

  • It combines satellite data, ground sensors, AI and voice in one tool built for farmers, not analysts.
  • The “Explain simply” feature and spoken daily briefings translate technical terms like NDVI and evapotranspiration into plain language.
  • The evidence-and-gaps panel and honest data labels build trust, rather than pretending the model is certain.
  • Scenario sliders let farmers ask “what if rainfall drops 20%?”

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy limits: NASA grids are coarse, so field values are estimates. Our sensors help fill this gap.
  • Honesty about data: NASA POWER soil wetness is model-based, not direct SMAP observation, and we label it that way.
  • Limits of the current version: rotation scoring is heuristic, not a validated agronomic prescription, and the AppEEARS time-series download is a planned next step.
  • Accessibility: multilingual, voice-enabled, mobile-first, with sample-data fallbacks and offline-friendly design for weak connectivity.
  • Safety: AI results show confidence levels and always recommend confirming with a local agronomist.
